text_boxes.text: ABSTRACT We examine 46,463 M ≥ 5 earthquakes using geographic reference points, equal-duration time comparisons and local depth sections. Events concentrate near mapped plate boundaries, but period differences also coincide with changes in catalogue composition. Regional depth tails and selected event sequences reveal structure that pooled summaries conceal. Our results describe a fixed catalogue; they do not estimate future hazard.

Earthquakes vary in location, depth, magnitude and timing. A map identifies clusters, yet it cannot explain whether they reflect geography, a few large sequences or changes in reporting. We connect these views to ask where recorded activity concentrates, how it varies over time, and which regional structures survive beyond global averages.

Coordinates, magnitude and depth are present for every record. Four negative reported depths are retained. Event IDs are deduplicated and non-earthquake types are excluded. A complete download does not prove complete earthquake detection, nor does a preferred magnitude represent one homogeneous scale.
Fig. 1. All epicentres on an equal-area Mollweide map; colours denote depth classes and grey lines PB2002 boundaries. Overlapping points are not area-normalized density.
Analytical strategy
Use one frozen sample, explicit denominators and sensitivity checks. Compare recorded patterns while keeping geological interpretation and measurement limitations separate.

Boundary proximity needs a geographic denominator. We compare earthquake distances with points uniformly distributed over Earth’s surface, including oceans. A second reference keeps the observed latitude distribution and varies longitude.
Fig. 2. Cumulative distance distributions use the same PB2002 arcs and spherical geometry (R = 6,371.0088 km) for events and both references.

70.15% of events lie within 100 km, compared with 9.42% of equal-area points and 10.50% of latitude-controlled points. The observed-to-area share ratio is 7.45. Thus, concentration remains clear under two geographic references; the ratio is not a risk multiplier or a causal effect.
Numerical and geological limits

Four independent 16,384-point designs give 9.38–9.53% within 100 km. This is numerical sensitivity, not a confidence interval. PB2002 is a simplified boundary layer, not a complete map of active faults.
Annual M ≥ 5 counts fluctuate substantially, peaking at 2,701 in 2011. Comparing equal 13-year periods gives a different summary from fitting a trend across the whole record.
Fig. 3. Annual counts and period means (dashed). Rate comparisons allow for 4,749 days in 2000–2012 and 4,748 days in 2013–2025.

The later-period record rate is 6.63% lower at M ≥ 5 and 15.42% lower at M ≥ 6. Yet the full-period M5 Sen slope is positive. Magnitude-type composition and error-field availability also change, so these contrasts alone cannot establish a change in physical seismic activity.
Regional and window sensitivity

M5 rate changes differ: Indonesia/Philippines −25.58%; Mediterranean/Himalaya +8.82%. Removing 30-day / 500-km windows around 28 M ≥ 8 events changes the global contrast to −3.37%. This is window sensitivity, not declustering.
Globally, 83.20% are shallow. Japan/Kuril and Tonga/Fiji share a 33 km median, but their deep-event shares differ by more than twofold.
Fig. 4. Maps: gold trench, blue route/swath, star at 0 km. A → B spans −200 to +1,200 km; swath ±100 km. Depth and distance use equal kilometre scales. Routes were selected after exploration.

Selected-section deep counts are 21/351 in northern Tohoku and 186/640 in central Tonga. Across the full regions, depth–boundary-distance Spearman ρ is +0.39 globally and +0.56 in Japan/Kuril. Magnitude associations are weak overall. These relationships describe patterns; pooled coefficients and illustrative sections do not identify a causal mechanism.
Event frequency and a magnitude-based energy proxy answer different questions. Their shares are compared directly below.

The 28 events at M ≥ 8 contribute 71.21% of the summed proxy, R(M)=101.5(M−5). One magnitude unit multiplies R by 31.6. Mixed preferred scales mean that this is illustrative, not measured joules, damage or risk.
Radius ≤500 km; UTC windows [−30,0) and [0,30) days from the exact anchor time. Anchors are excluded; all windows are fully observed.
Fig. 5. Each curve uses its own 30-day post-window total. Day d counts events in [0,d), separating timing from total counts.
Scope: These selections do not prove causal aftershock membership or a universal sequence law.

CONCLUSION Geography, regional depth tails and clustered sequences give a coherent descriptive picture. Time contrasts require catalogue-comparability checks; reference choices and window definitions remain central to interpretation. The strongest result is a transparent comparison of recorded patterns, not a forecast of future hazard.
